title: Ceann mhin's people will not climb to the ruin
summary: The households settled in sight of Làrach an Dùin ruin on the headland build their houses with their doors to the sea and their backs to the broken walls, and will not carry off the good dressed stone lying loose there for the taking, an old woman of that shore saying a wall raised by other hands keeps its own quarrel.

title: The smiths of the southern Seann Skell beat out hooks faster than the sea wears them
summary: Within a few generations of its resettling, the old harbour of the south becomes the busiest quay on that whole coast, boats going out on every tide and coming home heavy, and its smiths kept at the forge from first light beating out fish-hooks the fishing cannot outlast.

title: Achadh shean sinks its well before it breaks a furrow
summary: The households returning to the fields cracked by the long drought sink a new well deep into the rock before they plant a single seed, and tell it after as a lesson to their children: dig first, plant after, a well proved in a dry summer being worth more than an early harvest.

title: A boy of Inis mhin is lost among the egg-ledges
summary: A boy climbing after eggs is caught by dusk on a shelf below the cliff's highest nests, unhurt but unable to climb either way, and is brought up by torchlight on a rope woven that same night; afterward no one of that settlement works the cliffs alone, two to a rope by custom rather than any law spoken.

title: The first cairn rises above the fold at Muileann chaol
summary: When the head of one of the settling households dies, his kin carry stones up the slope above the cattle-fold and raise the first cairn there, one stone laid at a time by whoever had known him; within a lifetime the slope holds as many small heaps of stone as the fold below holds cattle in a good year.

title: Fearchar Bacach dies at Dùn ìseal
summary: Fearchar Bacach, who has held Dùn ìseal for the king since he was lamed in the passes long before, dies quietly in his own bed at three thousand one hundred and thirty years of age; his house keeps the hill after him without any household troubling to remark that it is being kept.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh settles ground its people call empty
summary: Households raise a broad red-earthed rise into Baile Mòr ruadh, a morning's walk from the old middens of Seann Dunn, calling the ground around them empty though the middens plainly say otherwise, and dig into nothing of what lies there.

title: A shepherd's flock will not cross the worn path at Làrach an Teampaill
summary: A shepherd wakes from a sun-warmed sleep to find his whole flock standing stock still along the path worn round Làrach an Teampaill, none grazing, none straying past its edge, and drives them home without letting a hoof cross it, telling after that his sheep had more sense of the place than he did.

title: Ìomhar is born to the king and called Dearg for his hair
summary: A son is born to the king in the south and named Ìomhar, called Dearg for hair redder than his father's or his brothers', who grows up about the southern shores and the eastern marches asking, before his first century is out, why a man may not simply be given ground and left to hold it.

title: Dòmhnall Clachach dies in the north country
summary: Dòmhnall Clachach, sent north from Dùn ìseal more than three thousand years before and known there only as the stone-cutter's son, dies among people who never troubled themselves with what he had once been, at three thousand three hundred and eight years of age; word of it reaches the hill a full season after the burying.

title: Alasdair Làidir takes every fall of the contests at three-and-twenty
summary: At the yearly contests below Clachan nan Gaoth of Ceann leathan, a young herdsman's son named Alasdair Làidir throws every man who stands against him from first light to last, the youngest ever known to do it, and is given by custom the first try at Clach a' Neirt that has never once been raised.

title: A grey stranger lifts the black boulder at Ceann leathan
summary: After Alasdair Làidir's strength fails against it, an unknown grey-haired traveller steps from the watching crowd, sets his hands to Clach a' Neirt and raises it to his knees, then sets it down again gently rather than dropping it, and walks off the headland refusing to give any name the reciters might carry.

title: The tale of the lifted stone wears smooth at other fires
summary: Carried from hearth to hearth along the southern coast, the tale of the grey stranger gains, within a few winters, a taller stranger, a one-handed lift and, at one fire near the southern Seann Skell, hands said to glow like a smith's iron, an embellishment Alasdair Làidir spends the rest of his life correcting wherever he hears it repeated.

title: An old woman at the ford sets a matching tale beside Alasdair's doubted one
summary: At the crowded ford gathering, an old man past his wrestling years tells, once more, of the stone lifted and gently set down at Ceann leathan; a grey-haired woman at the same fire answers his young doubters not by taking his side but by recalling a near-identical telling she heard thirty years before, from a different mouth entirely, at a fire near the southern Seann Skell.
